html:
The Atlantic slave trade carried enslaved Africans across the ocean to the Americas from the early 1500s to the 1860s. About 12.5 million people were put on ships. Roughly 10.7 million survived the crossing, known as the Middle Passage.

Portuguese traders began buying captives on the West African coast in the 1400s. The first direct voyages from Africa to the Americas came in the 1520s, and the trade grew with the sugar plantations of Brazil and the Caribbean. Brazil took more enslaved Africans than any other country. Britain, France, the Netherlands, Spain and the American colonies all joined in. Ships often ran a triangular route: goods from Europe to Africa, captives to the Americas, and sugar, tobacco and cotton back to Europe.

Most captives came from West and Central Africa. European traders rarely raided themselves; they bought people from African rulers and merchants. States such as Asante and Dahomey grew rich and strong on the trade, while the kingdom of Kongo was torn apart by it.

The end came slowly:

  • 1791: the Haitian Revolution began, the only slave revolt that founded a state.
  • 1807: Britain banned the trade and later used its navy against it. The United States banned imports in 1808.
  • 1860s: the last known voyages landed in Cuba.
  • 1888: Brazil abolished slavery, the last country in the Americas to do so.

The trade linked three continents. It made fortunes in Europe, emptied regions of Africa, and gave the Americas much of their population and culture. It belongs with the Columbian Exchange as the force that made the Atlantic world.
